Action Plan:
1. Schedule face-to-face clinic visit within 4–5 days for otoscopic examination to rule out impacted cerumen or other external/middle-ear pathology causing left-sided hearing loss.  
2. Send tinnitus patient-information leaflet link; patient to review before clinic visit.  
3. Patient to phone support team (number left in visit notes) today to secure appointment slot.  
4. Safety-netting: advised to book urgent video/telephone review if hearing worsens, dizziness becomes severe, or new symptoms (pain, discharge, fever, chest pain, palpitations) develop before scheduled visit.  
5. Verbal consent from patient has been obtained before using transcription software.

Subjective:
• Presenting complaint: Reduced hearing in left ear for 6 weeks.  
• Course: Intermittent; occasionally triggered/worsened by TV or music.  
• Associated symptoms: Intermittent left-sided tinnitus; mild episodic dizziness/off-balance sensation without true vertigo or nausea; no pain, discharge, itching, fever, chest pain, or palpitations.  
• Laterality: Right ear normal.  
• Past similar episode: Brief 2-day episode ≈1 year ago, resolved spontaneously.  
• Past medical history: not discussed.  
• Medications: not discussed.  
• Allergies: not discussed.  
• Social history: not discussed.  
• Ear-care habits: Does not use cotton buds.

Objective:
(No physical examination performed during video consult; no vitals available.)

Assessment & Plan:

1. Left-sided hearing loss  
   - Likely diagnosis: Conductive hearing loss secondary to possible impacted cerumen or other external/middle-ear pathology.  
   - Investigations: Otoscopic examination at in-person visit.  
   - Treatment: If wax present, remove per clinic protocol; further management guided by findings.  

2. Left-sided tinnitus  
   - Likely diagnosis: Tinnitus (idiopathic vs secondary to ear pathology).  
   - Investigations: As above (otoscopic exam). Consider audiometry if symptoms persist after wax exclusion.  
   - Treatment: Provided tinnitus education leaflet; discuss management options after examination results.  
   - Referral: Consider ENT/audiology if persistent after initial assessment.  

3. Episodic mild dizziness/off-balance  
   - Likely diagnosis: Vestibular disturbance secondary to same ear pathology.  
   - Differential: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, vestibular neuritis, Ménière’s disease (less likely without vertigo or nausea).  
   - Investigations: Clinical review following ear examination; further vestibular testing if indicated.  
   - Treatment: Reassurance and monitoring; escalate if severity increases.  

Quality checks:
● Missing elements: allergies, current medications, past medical/surgical history, social history, vitals, formal audiometry.  
● No internal transcript conflicts noted.  
● Transcript quality: clear, occasional minor gaps but clinically adequate.
